rows.evidence: Q1: Methodology section <U+2013> 10 pilot household farms received drip kits plus hand-dug wells, 50 non-pilot farms as control; crop yield and water productivity collected, plus questionnaires and focus groups with 60 respondents in three kebeles. Q2: Section 3.4, Figures 9<U+2013>10 <U+2013> the drip intervention raised yields by 56 to 120% for all crops except maize relative to the traditional surface-irrigated, communal-well farms. Q7: Section 3.5 and Section 4 <U+2013> from farmer-reported challenges (maintenance of lines and wells, no kits in local markets, skills, investment) the authors state that technical and financial support, capacity building and market access are needed for efficient use of the drip systems and improvement of yields. Q8: Section 4 <U+2013> the authors state the study did not account for socio-economic and biophysical factors (soil types and depths, nutrients, landscape, rainfall patterns); Methodology also notes the comparison assumed fertilizer, seed and management were similar.
rows.notes: Yield effect is for drip combined with private hand-dug wells versus surface irrigation from communal wells, so the drip effect is confounded with improved water supply; tomato is not among the crops studied (potatoes, carrots, garlic, onions, cabbage, maize) and only potato results are highlighted. Q3: survey comments that the system improves yields are general perceptions, not an independent quantification of the yield effect; rated no. Q4: a figure of ~65% uniform water distribution is mentioned without method; water productivity said to be collected but not presented; rated no. Q5: three kebeles in one district, yield results not reported per kebele. Q6: results at 0.5 ha household plot level, no scheme/district-level result. Q9: 56<U+2013>120% is a range across crops, no SD/CI; yields measured only once in one season.

notes: Full text appears complete; figures and tables not included, so numeric detail is limited to what the text states.
